messages.subject: Measuring distance in 3-dementions
parts:
I'm developing a pilot study to estimate abundance and density of black
rockfish along a section of coastline in south-central Alaska. I'll be
evaluating the use of mark-resighting closed population models and line
transect sampling to obtain independent estimates and to evaluate bias.
I'll be using SCUBA to do both. Black rockfish are a pelagic species
commonly associated with bottom habitats but can occur off bottom. They are
a schooling species so I may end up counting schools and estimating school
size instead of counting individual fish. My main question is what is the
best technique to measure distance to an individual or school if the fish
are distributed 3-dementionally? If I draw an imaginary line vertically to
the transect line and measure the perpendicular distance from myself to fish
both on the bottom and fish off the bottom than I'm dealing with a volume.
Alternatively, I could estimate the perpendicular distance from the
"imaginary vertical line" to the fish, whether they are off the bottom or
not. This in my mind adds another delectability function, since not all
fish at a given perpendicular distance to the "imaginary vertical line" are
the same distance to the observer. I could minimize this by swimming off
bottom a bit and ignoring fish that are and equal distance above me. Do you
have suggestions?

Thanks, Mike
mike_...@fishgame.state.ak.us

Mike, you'll find theory for 3D line transects in the 1993 distance
sampling book. Unfortunately, we can't assume that animals are uniformly
distributed with respect to distance from the line in the vertical
direction in your (or most) applications. This complicates things, but
can in principle be addressed. I'm not aware though that anyone has
developed, or is devloping, this methodology. We have not pursued it
partly because we felt that it would not be relevant to the vast majority
of users of Distance (and partly through lack of funds!). It might make a
nice PhD project for someone though.

What can you do meantime? Provided you can ensure that the majority of
fish on or near the 'line' (which is now a 2D plane, from the bottom
vertically up to the surface) are detected, you can just record horizontal
distances from this plane, and analyse the data in the usual way. Three
approaches occur to me, which may or may not be workable for your study:

a) do one survey for fish on the bottom, then a separate survey for fish
off the bottom. Add the 2 abundance estimates together.

b) use 2 (or more) SCUBA divers, one covering bottom fish, and the
other(s) covering fish off the bottom, to ensure g(0) is close to 1.

c) survey bottom fish only; separately conduct a survey to estimate the
proportion of time spent on the bottom by monitoring a sample of fish. If
this proportion is p, and estimated density of fish on the bottom is D,
then the estimated density (numbers per unit area of sea) is D/p. Of
course, this can be converted to numbers per unit volume if you feel that
makes more sense, but I would tend to stick with D.
